title: Madlener–Otto plain-group conjecture
formal: Let A be a finite alphabet and R a finite confluent length-reducing string-rewriting system. If the quotient monoid \(A^*/{\equiv_R}\) is a group G, must there be finite groups \(H_1,\ldots,H_s\) and an integer r≥0 with \[G\cong H_1*\cdots*H_s*F_r\,?\]
definitions:
A* is the monoid of finite words, including the empty word, with concatenation. A rule u→v is a pair of words with |u|>|v|. A rewrite step replaces an occurrence of u inside any word by v. Write →* for zero or more steps. Confluence means that if w→*x and w→*y, some z satisfies x→*z and y→*z. Strict length decrease guarantees that every sequence terminates; these two properties give a unique irreducible word for each congruence class. The congruence ≡_R is the least equivalence relation respecting concatenation and identifying each rule’s two sides. The quotient is assumed to be a group under the induced multiplication.

The alphabet is not required to contain a one-letter representative of each generator’s inverse. Right-hand sides may have any finite length smaller than the corresponding left-hand side. There is no bound shared across all input systems on rule lengths or number of rules. F_r is the free group of finite rank r; * is the group free product. Empty lists of finite factors and rank zero are permitted, covering finite, free and trivial groups. Groups with such a decomposition are called plain. The question asks only the implication from a presentation to this structural decomposition, not an efficient recognition algorithm.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every finite system satisfying the hypotheses, or exhibit one finite system and prove confluence, strict length reduction, the group property, and failure of every plain decomposition. A result assuming inverse-closed generators or a bound on right-hand-side lengths does not settle the general statement.
context:
The Madlener–Otto conjecture relates a finite normal-form presentation to a rigid group decomposition. The unrestricted alphabet matters: inverse-closed presentations form a special case.

Elder and Piggott give structural and computational criteria in the inverse-closed case, rather than a proof that all groups in the unrestricted class are plain.
why: The conjecture would characterize exactly which group word problems admit this finite normalization mechanism.
